catalog_quote: Many younger people can greet and give simple commands in Hozo, but struggle when it comes to the narration of a longer story or the elaboration of a complex argument because their vocabulary is not large enough or is limited to a few domains. They may show uncertainties in the use of grammatical forms and especially in the correct use of tones, which have both semantically and morphologically distinctive functions in the language. [Supporting, Küspert 2015: 60, fn. 140, on the Seze column of the Seze/Hozo/Ganza/Gwama/Komo word list:] Girma Mengistu: káwwì; cf. ‘arm’; tone difference; tones may be distinctive in all “Mao-Komo languages”, but are not written here because of poor data. [Supporting, Ahland 2019: 190, section 3.3 Hoozo:] In Hoozo (unlike in Mawes Aas’e and Seezo), morphological case marking on subjects and objects tends to be limited to NPs preceded by definite articles or demonstratives ... (Kassa 2015:95-97). Hoozo’s subject and object case markers are sensitive to gender and are distinguished only by toneː /-já/ SBJ.M, /-jé/ SBJ.F, /-jà/ OBJ.M, and /-jè/ OBJ.F (Kassa 2015:95).

In that raw file the sentence sits in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hozo is described as a tone language in which tone distinguishes both lexical items and grammatical forms; no source opened says anything about word stress or its position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Note that Küspert 2015 fn. 190 'Stress on last vowel.' (p. 63) belongs to the Seze column of the wordlist ('two' nɔmbe), not to Hozo.
new_statements.domain_note: The 2022 statement is a sociolinguistic remark (speakers' uncertainty in 'the correct use of tones'), not a phonological description; no domain (word vs phrase) is specified. The 2015 note is a wordlist footnote covering the whole 'Mao-Komo' group tentatively.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the Hozo/Hoozo of the Begi–Kondala area (autonym Ak'mo Wandi; Küspert 2015 also 'Shuluyo' as a variety/clan name) = hozo1236. Not to be confused with Seze/Sezo (seze1238) or Northern/Bambassi Mao (bamb1262, Ahland 2012). The 'Stress on last vowel' footnote in Küspert 2015 is a Seze datum.

tone_statements.citation: Ahland, Michael. 2022 (author's final manuscript, dated 21 Dec 2022; forthcoming). Omotic Features in the Mao Group and Internal Coherence. Chapter prepared for the Oxford Guide to the Afroasiatic Languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press. 36 pp. (MS). Open author copy, California State University, Long Beach.
tone_statements.quote: All four of the Mao languages are tonal. Hoozo, Seezo, and Ganza exhibit two underlying levels (H and L). [...] The Hoozo language uses tone for various grammatical functions, including the difference between nominative and accusative case (-já NOM.M and -jé NOM.F vs. -jà ACC.M -jè ACC.F), modality and evidential marking (e.g. -é irrealis vs. -è subjective evidential) and pronominal distinctions (e.g. hí 2SG vs. the interrogative hì ‘whatʼ); For the full discussion, see Getachew Kassa’s overview, 2015:76-78).
tone_statements.locator: Author's MS p. 2, section 3.1.1.1 'Tonal Contrasts, Major Features, and Historical Links' (first sentence pair); MS p. 9, section 3.1.1.2 'Tone as a Marker of Stem Type in Mao' (grammatical functions); stem-tone pairs ex. (23)-(24) on MS p. 8
tone_statements.summary: Two underlying level tones (H, L) with both lexical and grammatical function: tone alone separates verb vs noun stems and marks case (H nominative vs L accusative suffixes), mood/evidentiality and pronoun contrasts; data secondhand from Getachew Kassa 2015.

sources.note: Survey/classification paper with 38/78-item wordlists. No stress statement for Hozo. Footnote 140, p. 60 (Appendix 3 wordlist): 'tone difference; tones may be distinctive in all "Mao-Komo languages", but are not written here because of poor data.' Footnote 190, p. 63, 'Stress on last vowel.' is attached to the Seze column ('two' nɔmbe), not to Hozo (Hozo 'two' is dɔmbɔ in the next column).

sources.note: States the Hoozo tone inventory and functions explicitly: Hoozo (like Seezo and Ganza) has two underlying tone levels, H and L (vs. Mawes Aas'e with three surface levels / four underlying tones); tone distinguishes verbal from nominal stems (ʔííʃí 'call' vs ʔííʃì 'name', màà 'eat' vs máá 'food', Kassa 2015:80; gerund pì-pə́llì with reduplication plus tone change) and carries grammatical functions: nominative vs accusative case suffixes differing only in tone (-já/-jé NOM vs -jà/-jè ACC), irrealis -é vs subjective evidential -è, hí 2SG vs hì 'what' (Kassa 2015:76-78); terminal vowels /i/, /a/…
